notes: Digital cards: rendered on-device at 6x4 in (1800x1200 px at 300 dpi), single-sided by default with an optional back. Players can save, share, print or make their own. Images are fetched at build time from image_direct_url and bundled with the content feed; nothing is hot-linked at runtime. Each pack's digital cards unlock on that pack's own rules. Physical cards: the `physical` block - one Alarm Club postcard set, the same for everyone, earned the first time a player finishes any walk (Richard, Oct 12 2026, final). See POSTCARDS.md.

physical.admin_note: To stop: close the Google Form first (Responses > Accepting responses off), then set offered to false and push - the block disappears on each phone's next sync. Dedupe by address in the responses sheet: one set per address. Never show a quantity. Form text: handoff/POSTCARD-FORM.md.

copy.locked_line: Finish any walk - any route, a short cut counts - and we'll mail you the Alarm Club postcards. Free.

unlock_alternative_considered.all_packs_complete: Rejected Oct 11: 20-plus hours of walking and $6.99 of purchases before a free mailer.
unlock_alternative_considered.one_set_per_pack: Tried and dropped Oct 12 2026: eleven sets made finishing a paid pack earn a physical reward the free packs couldn't, a purchase incentive. One set for everyone is literally no pay.
unlock_alternative_considered.the_1852_hunt_only: The rule until Oct 12 2026. Replaced by any walk, so Shot Here players and paid-pack players get the same set.

physical.unlock_rule_note: Earned the first time the player finishes any route of any pack - full route or short cut, free pack or paid. One set per player. Finishing more walks earns nothing more physically. The free walks (The 1852 Hunt, Shot Here) earn exactly the same set, so paying never earns anything extra. Field-check finishes don't count (the button shows on that session's Finale, nothing is saved).

postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Report of the Commissioners appointed to investigate the cause and management of the Great Fire in Boston (1873), pp.12, 42, 391
Boston Fire Historical Society, Great Boston Fire of 1872
Boston Public Library blog, The Great Boston Fire of 1872

postcards.back_text: On November 9, 1872, Officer John Page heard boys yelling fire on Summer Street and figured they were doing it to plague him. Then he saw the flames, took out his own key and opened Box 52. The alarm was logged at 7:24 - a quarter of an hour after the fire was first seen. By the next day 776 buildings were gone. Why it was late is still open.

front.credit: Geo. W. Reynolds, 'Boston Fire of 1872, remains of Claflin Larrabee building,' ca. 1872. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, via Digital Commonwealth.
front.crop_note: Albumen print, 4 3/4 x 8 in - already wider than 6x4, so crop the sides, not the top. Keep the full height of the standing walls; trim the print's mount edges. Do not tint or colorize. Check the frame after download - nobody on this team has seen it at full size yet.

postcards.title: The Box That Was Late

postcards.back_credit_line: Front: N. L. Stebbins, 'Tremont Street subway explosion,' March 4, 1897. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, via Digital Commonwealth.
postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Third Annual Report of the Boston Transit Commission (1897)
City of Boston Archives, Notes from the Archives: Tremont Street Subway
N. L. Stebbins photograph and verso caption, Boston Public Library

postcards.back_text: On March 4, 1897, gas leaking into the subway dig blew up the corner of Tremont and Boylston, six months before America's first subway opened. The Transit Commission's own report counts six dead at the scene and four more afterward, then adds one line: 'The subway structure was not injured.' The subway opened that September.

front.credit: N. L. Stebbins, 'Tremont Street subway explosion,' March 4, 1897. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, via Digital Commonwealth.
front.crop_note: Print is 7 1/2 x 9 1/2 in. If it is portrait, use a landscape crop across the street scene, or set it as a portrait card - either is fine at 6x4. People died here: no tight crop on any figure, no red overlay, no 'boom' styling. Plain frame.
front.license: No Copyright - United States. BPL: 'No known copyright restrictions. No known restrictions on use.' Verified on source page Oct 11 2026.

postcards.title: The Subway Structure Was Not Injured

postcards.back_credit_line: Front: Southworth & Hawes, 'Use of ether at the Massachusetts General Hospital, 1847.' Wellcome Collection. Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Mass Moments (Mass Humanities), Boston Dentist Demonstrates Ether: October 16, 1846
Paul S. Russell, MD Museum of Medical History and Innovation (MGH), About The Ether Dome
Wellcome Collection, Use of ether at the Massachusetts General Hospital, 1847

postcards.back_text: On October 16, 1846, under the dome at Mass General, dentist William Morton held an ether inhaler to a young printer named Gilbert Abbott. Surgeon John Collins Warren cut a tumor from his neck and told the room, 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug.' This is not that day. Wellcome Collection dates this daguerreotype by Southworth & Hawes to 1847, a year later, at the same hospital.

front.credit: Southworth & Hawes, 'Use of ether at the Massachusetts General Hospital, 1847.' Wellcome Collection. Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
front.crop_note: Daguerreotype: keep the plate's tarnish and mat edge rather than cleaning it up. Crop to the group around the table; do not crop into the patient. CC BY allows cropping - note 'cropped' in the credit if you crop. Other copies exist (MGH, Harvard, the Met); use only this Wellcome scan unless another holder's license is checked.
front.license: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Verified on source page Oct 11 2026. Attribution required on the card - the credit line below is Wellcome's own wording.

postcards.back_credit_line: Front: Boston Board of Health, 'Map showing the sources of some of the offensive odors perceived in Boston,' 1878. Wm. M. Coombs del. Norman B. Leventhal Map & Education Center at the Boston Public Library.
postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Leventhal Map & Education Center, Map showing the sources of some of the offensive odors perceived in Boston, 1878
Ian Spangler, Of Odors and Esplanades, Leventhal Map & Education Center (2022), citing Seasholes, Gaining Ground p.215

postcards.back_text: In 1878 Boston's Board of Health mapped the city's smells: sewer outlets, mud-sewage flats, offensive trades, and the districts each wind carried them to. An engineer quoted by historian Nancy Seasholes called the flats where Stony Brook met the Muddy River 'the filthiest marsh and mud flats to be found anywhere in Massachusetts.' Olmsted's fix was the Fens, and he insisted nobody call it a park.

front.credit: Boston Board of Health, 'Map showing the sources of some of the offensive odors perceived in Boston,' 1878. Wm. M. Coombs del. Norman B. Leventhal Map & Education Center at the Boston Public Library.
front.crop_note: Color map, 43 x 56 cm, north to the upper right. Two good crops: the whole sheet (title readable at 6x4? check) or a detail on the Back Bay and the Fens with the mud-sewage flats and the legend. Do not rotate north-up - the tilt is part of it. Work from the TIF for a detail crop.

Keith N. Morgan, Logan Airport, SAH Archipedia (Buildings of Massachusetts)

postcards.back_text: This is Boston's airport in 1923: 189 acres off Jeffries Point and two cinder runways about 1,500 feet long. A note on the back of this print says the first landing was June 13, 1923, by Lt. Kitchell Snow. The Massachusetts Aviation Historical Society says a pair of draft horses dragged a wooden sledge over the cinders to smooth them. It got bigger.

front.credit: U.S. Army Air Service, 'Logan - Boston. Then called Commonwealth Airport - Boston,' 1923. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, Boston Pictorial Archive.
front.crop_note: Gelatin silver aerial, 6 3/4 x 9 in - close to 6x4 already. Keep both runways in frame; if the T layout is visible, center it. Leave any handwriting on the print face in.

back_sources.title: Amtrak, Great American Stations: Boston, MA - South Station (BOS)

Ty Burr, Reel Boston, The Boston Globe (2005)

postcards.back_text: South Station opened on New Year's Day 1899, two years before this picture. In 1965 the city bought it and decided to knock it down, and a 1972 Boston Globe Magazine story reported the plan to clear the rest. It went on the National Register in 1975 instead. The Globe's list of Boston film locations puts it in The Thomas Crown Affair in 1967 and The Verdict in 1982. Nobody had to build this one on a soundstage.

front.credit: 'Dewey Square' (also catalogued 'Dewey Square and South Station'), 1901. Boston Public Library, Boston Pictorial Archive, via Digital Commonwealth.
front.crop_note: Print 7 3/4 x 9 3/4 in; scan 3164 x 2508, landscape - close to 6x4. Keep the station's curved corner and the clock in frame; crop sky or street, not the top of the headhouse. Nobody on this team has seen it at full size - confirm the station is the subject before shipping. Not a film still: this is a 1901 BPL photograph.

postcards.back_credit_line: Front: Thomas E. Marr, 'Park Street Church, looking north, April 1, 1906.' Boston Public Library, Arts Department, via Digital Commonwealth.
postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Mass Moments, H.L. Mencken Arrested in Boston (April 5, 1926)
H.L. Mencken, To the friends of the American Mercury (Boston, 1926), with the opinion of Justice James P. Parmenter - HathiTrust
The Phoenix, On this day in 1926: Boston, H.L. Mencken, and the landmark free-speech case that wasn't (2010)
Boston Public Library, Park Street Church, looking north, April 1, 1906

postcards.back_text: Twenty years after this picture, on April 5, 1926, H.L. Mencken stood on this corner with the April issue of his American Mercury and waited for the Watch and Ward Society, which had called it obscene. Its secretary, J. Frank Chase, paid a silver half dollar for a copy. Mencken bit the coin, the story goes, and Chase had him arrested. The next day a judge acquitted him, and Mencken printed the opinion himself.

front.credit: Thomas E. Marr, 'Park Street Church, looking north, April 1, 1906.' Boston Public Library, Arts Department, via Digital Commonwealth.
front.crop_note: Print 7 1/2 x 9 3/4 in; scan 4250 x 3320, landscape. Catalogued as 'Tremont St.: Corner of the Common, Park St. Church to right, State House to left' - keep the church steeple and the sidewalk at the corner; that sidewalk is the stage. Same image as the pack's then-and-now at banned-in-boston-02. Leave the negative number on the print face if it shows.

postcards.back_text: Around 1879 Sarah Howe opened the Ladies' Deposit in the South End: single women only, eight percent a month, backed, she said, by Quakers. The Atlantic said she had no more hold upon the Quakers than upon the Pope. She lived across Franklin Square from the St. James Hotel, the building on the front. In 1881 she got three years. Forty years later a man on School Street ran the same play and got the name.

If a printed title is on the mount, it can stay below the image or go - either way, not cropped mid-word.

postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Mass Moments, Codnapping at House of Representatives (April 26, 1933)

Sacred Cod - Wikipedia (lead; follow citations)

postcards.back_text: On April 26, 1933, three Harvard Lampoon editors walked into the State House with wire clippers and a florist's box and walked out with the Sacred Cod, the carved wooden fish that hangs over the House chamber. Police dragged the Charles. Two nights later it was handed back in the woods off the West Roxbury Parkway. It went back up on April 29, about six inches higher. Nobody was charged.

front.credit: 'Boston, Massachusetts. State House. House of Representatives,' ca. 1880-1900. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, Boston Pictorial Archive.
front.crop_note: Albumen print 7 1/2 x 9 1/2 in; scan only 2240 x 1770 - enough for 1800 x 1200, no more, so crop lightly. The print's own note reads 'State House, House of Representatives, gallery. Built 1889-94.' Nobody on this team has seen it at full size: if the cod is in frame, keep it in; if it isn't, the caption and back still hold (neither says the fish is in the picture).

postcards.back_credit_line: Front: 'Symphony Hall, Boston, Mass.,' Detroit Publishing Co., c1904. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-DIG-det-4a11361.
postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: National Historic Landmark Nomination: Symphony Hall, National Park Service
Boston Symphony Orchestra, A Timeline of Symphony Hall
Symphony Hall, Boston - Wikipedia
Library of Congress, Symphony Hall, Boston, Mass. (Detroit Publishing Co., c1904)

postcards.back_text: Symphony Hall opened on October 15, 1900, with its front door on Huntington Avenue; the Massachusetts Avenue side was for carriages. Henry Lee Higginson hired Wallace Clement Sabine, then an assistant professor of physics at Harvard, to work out how sound would behave in the room. The National Historic Landmark nomination calls it the very first concert hall designed on scientific acoustic principles. Other accounts say one of the first. Over the stage, one name: Beethoven.

front.credit: 'Symphony Hall, Boston, Mass.,' Detroit Publishing Co., c1904. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-DIG-det-4a11361.
front.crop_note: 8 x 10 in glass dry-plate negative (Detroit Publishing no. 017045). Fetch the TIF - the large JPEG is only about 1024 px, too small for 1800 x 1200. Landscape; keep the full facade and roofline. Which side of the hall it shows (Huntington Avenue front or Massachusetts Avenue carriage side) is not recorded - check before writing any caption that names the side. Same image as the pack's stop image at loud-boston-09.

postcards.back_credit_line: Front: Leander Baker, 'Parker House, School Street,' stereograph, ca. 1850-1920. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, Stereograph Collection, via Digital Commonwealth.
postcards.back_footer: Off the Bricks - A Third Polar Arch project

back_sources.title: Yankee Magazine, Boston Cream Pie | Recipe with a History, with comment by Susan Wilson, House Historian, Omni Parker House (Feb 25 2019)
Omni Parker House, History
Massachusetts General Laws, c.2 s.41: Dessert or dessert emblem of commonwealth
CooksInfo, Boston Cream Pie
Omni Hotels: The Parker House (hotel plaque), HMdb m21664 - current building erected 1927

postcards.back_text: For decades the story went that a French chef named Sanzian invented Boston cream pie at the Parker House in 1856. In 2019 Susan Wilson, the hotel's own house historian, wrote that there never was a chef named Sanzian. The famous French chef was Augustine Anezin, who cooked there from 1865, so 1856 is 'simply impossible.' The pie is real. Since 1996 it has been the official dessert of the Commonwealth.

front.credit: Leander Baker, 'Parker House, School Street,' stereograph, ca. 1850-1920. Boston Public Library, Arts Department, Stereograph Collection, via Digital Commonwealth.
front.crop_note: Stereo card, 9 x 18 cm; scan 4191 x 2125 is the whole card with both frames. Use ONE frame (left or right, whichever is cleaner), cropped to 6x4 - the frame is near square, so trim top and bottom, keep the hotel's School Street front. Don't use the full double image, don't use the card's back (the record's second image).
